key_insight: This paper tackles a practical gap in multi-modal learning: models often fail when some modalities are missing at training or test time. Its core idea is to use co-learning so information from available modalities can help compensate for missing arbitrary modalities, beyond the usual bimodal setting.
problem_solved: It addresses multi-modal classification under inconsistent modality availability caused by real-world issues such as sensor failures, privacy limits, or deployment constraints. The goal is to make classification models more robust when any subset of modalities may be absent.
method: Adopts a multi-modal co-learning framework instead of relying only on robust fusion across fixed modality pairs.
Designed to handle arbitrary missing modalities, not just simple bimodal missingness.
Uses information from observed modalities during learning to improve performance when modality patterns differ between training and inference.
impact: For practitioners, this means multi-modal systems can be deployed more reliably in messy real-world settings where inputs are incomplete. It supports stronger generalization and reduces performance drops when data sources are unavailable.
visual_elements: A pipeline diagram showing training vs. inference with missing modalities highlighted
A modality matrix illustrating arbitrary missingness across samples
A co-learning diagram linking multiple modalities through shared supervision
A performance chart comparing baseline fusion methods vs. the proposed approach under missing-modality conditions
paper_title: Co-Learning for Missing Arbitrary Modalities in Multi-modal Classification
paper_authors: Francisco Mena, Dino Ienco, Roberto Interdonato, Cassio F. Dantas, Simon Besnard
